analysis.one_liner: Caps federal tax on basic living costs for low- and middle-income workers, funded by a surcharge on million-dollar incomes.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in March 2026 by Senator Van Hollen with 20 cosponsors, has sat in the Senate Finance Committee with no hearing, markup, or vote scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill creates a new ceiling on federal income tax for workers at low and middle incomes: their tax cannot exceed 25.5% of the income they earn above a 'cost-of-living exemption,' which starts at about $46,000 for a single worker and rises with inflation. For most people under the cap, that means the income needed to cover basic living expenses is effectively tax-free. To pay for it, the bill adds a new surcharge of 5% to 12% on individuals' income above $1 million.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and families below roughly 175% of the cost-of-living exemption — about $80,500 for a single filer, $161,000 for a joint return, and $112,700 for a head of household under the bill's formula — would see their federal income tax cut, in some cases to zero, because the first ~$46,000 (adjusted for family size and inflation) of income would be exempt from any tax.

how_it_helps.text: The bill caps the tax of a 'qualified individual' at 25.5% of income above a cost-of-living exemption, meaning a single worker's first $46,000 of income (indexed to inflation) carries no federal income tax at all [S2].

Eligibility reaches far up the income scale: anyone with modified income below 175% of the exemption qualifies, which works out to roughly $80,500 for a single filer, $161,000 for a joint return, and $112,700 for a head of household [S2].

The bill is paid for by a new surcharge on high incomes: 5% on income between $1 million and $2 million, 10% between $2 million and $5 million, and 12% above $5 million, with higher thresholds for joint filers [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Individuals (not corporations) with modified income over $1 million — about $1.5 million for joint filers — would pay the new surcharge, which applies to all individual income including investment and pass-through business income, and would disallow the investment interest deduction above those thresholds.

drawbacks.text: The surcharge reaches business and investment income reported on individual returns, so owners of partnerships, S-corporations, and large investment portfolios would face a higher combined federal rate; opponents of similar surcharges argue this raises taxes on some small and family businesses [S2].

Joint filers get thresholds 1.5 times the single filer amounts rather than double, so two-earner couples in high-cost areas can face a marriage penalty at the surcharge thresholds and around the cap's eligibility line [S2].

The bill counts previously untaxed Social Security benefits in the income measure used for the cap; for most beneficiaries the cap still lowers their bill, but it could limit the benefit for some older filers with modest outside income [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct trade-off is clean: a broad tax cut for workers below roughly $80,000–$161,000 of income, funded entirely by a new 5–12% surcharge on about the top half of one percent of households. The main honest objections are that the surcharge reaches some pass-through business income and that the joint-filer thresholds are not fully doubled. The bill contains no other revenue mechanism or spending, so if the surcharge proved to raise less than the cut costs, the difference would add to deficits.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: Senator Van Hollen introduced the bill on March 12, 2026, joined by 19 other senators as original cosponsors [S1].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, which is the standard first step for a tax bill [S4].
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — appears in the bill's action history [S4].
All 20 cosponsors are Democrats or independents; the list includes both of the Senate's independents and 18 of its 45 Democrats [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far the outcome is simply inaction: the workers who would get the tax cut remain under current law, and high-income households avoid the new surcharge. Whoever controls the Senate Finance Committee's calendar — currently the Republican majority — is better positioned, since the bill advances only if they choose to act on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners, so far — the bill has not advanced

for.name: Sen. Chris Van Hollen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 19 original cosponsors.

for.name: 2 of 2 Senate independents
for.what_they_did: Both independents in the Senate cosponsored the bill.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (Chair Mike Crapo)
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by the majority party
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction; no hearing, markup, or committee vote appears on the record.

against.name: Senate Republican majority
against.role: 55 of 100 senators; controls the chamber's floor agenda
against.what_they_did: No Republican senator cosponsored the bill, and the majority has not scheduled it for floor action.

sides.party_line_note: Every supporter is a Democrat or independent — 21 of the Senate's 47 Democratic and independent members — while no Republican cosponsored and the 55-member Republican majority controls whether the bill moves.

industries.note: The bill imposes a new 5–12% surcharge on their income above $1 million (higher thresholds for joint filers), which is what pays for the tax cut for workers. Their cost in this bill is the public's benefit, dollar for dollar.

industries.industry: Owners of pass-through businesses and large investment portfolios
industries.note: Because the surcharge applies to individual income, business profits reported on personal returns and investment income are covered, and the bill disallows the investment interest deduction in computing it.
The bill explicitly exempts charitable trusts from the surcharge, leaving their tax treatment unchanged.

analysis.trajectory: A tax bill with no Republican cosponsors sits with a Finance Committee chaired by the majority party. Unless its provisions are attached to a broader tax package, the likely path is no hearing or vote before this Congress ends — the usual fate for partisan tax bills in the minority's control.
